headline: UK medical cannabis: 2.34 million items in a year, adviser warns
dek: At a London symposium on 26 November, Prof. Trevor Jones called UK prescribing growth disturbing, as industry urged a bigger role for nurses.
key_points: Prof. Trevor Jones, co-chair of the UK Cannabinoid R&D Group, said 2.34 million items were dispensed in a single year, more than the 1.54 million of the previous five years combined.
Eight years after rescheduling, only three cannabis-based medicines are licensed for prescription in the UK; most patients use unlicensed products from private clinics.

The Cannabis Industry Council published a paper on 25 November urging clinics to expand nursing roles; nurse prescribers wrote 25,947 items from January 2019 to May 2025, against 955,471 by pharmacists.
Curaleaf Laboratories launched a free CPD-accredited education platform for prescribers, and patient and police speakers said driving remains the biggest legal risk for patients.
body: The UK's private medical cannabis market has grown faster than the evidence, the rules and the prescriber workforce around it. That was the message from a sold-out Cannabis Health Symposium at Conway Hall in London on 26 November, according to live coverage by Business of Cannabis. The sharpest warning came from Professor Trevor Jones, co-chair of the UK Cannabinoid R&D Group, who said 2.34 million items were dispensed in a single year, more than the 1.54 million prescribed across the previous five years combined. He called the trend rather disturbing.

The day before, the Cannabis Industry Council (CIC), a UK trade body, published a policy paper arguing that trained nurses are the sector's most underused clinical resource. Taken together, the two events describe a market that is large and growing quickly, but still leans on a narrow group of prescribers and on unlicensed products.

The symposium opened with Cannabis Health editor Sarah Sinclair putting the patient base at an estimated 100,000 people and noting that the Care Quality Commission, the health regulator for England, counted more than 1 million items prescribed in England last year. Evidence, trials, clinician education and NHS access have not kept pace, she said.

Jones, a former director general of the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry and a former R&D director at Wellcome, said only three cannabis-based medicines are approved for prescription eight years after the UK rescheduled cannabis, and most patients receive unlicensed products from private clinics. He cited a case of one prescriber who signed 26,000 items in March 2026. Business of Cannabis noted NHS Business Services Authority caveats: an item is not the same as a prescription or a patient, and active prescriber identifiers rose from 116 to 200 between 2022 and 2024.

Jones called for one accountable figure in government, centralised research through the National Institute for Health and Care Research, and confirmation from the Home Office that CBD can be purified to a regulatory standard. He also doubted that the forthcoming review by the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs would be comprehensive.
> The UK built a cannabis market through private clinics, not through licensed medicines. The prescribing data is now forcing that choice into the open.

The CIC paper, written by Ariana Ayu, founder of the US-based CannyNurse Certificate Programme, was presented at the symposium by Adam Windish, the council's lead on standards, awareness and education. Business of Cannabis reported its key figures. From January 2019 to May 2025, pharmacist independent prescribers accounted for 955,471 items, or 61.9%; doctors for 553,218, or 35.8%; and nurse prescribers for just 25,947. On our arithmetic, nurses wrote under 2% of items.

The paper points out that nurse independent prescribers regulated by the Nursing and Midwifery Council have been able to prescribe unlicensed medicines since 2009 and controlled drugs within their competence since 2012. It cites the CQC's 2025 update, which recorded a 134% year-on-year rise in independent-sector prescribing to 833,525 items, and CIC estimates of 75,000 to 90,000 patients treated in 2025. It makes four recommendations for clinics: invest in recognised specialist nursing education, build nurses into clinical pathways, set up clinical governance and escalation procedures, and create nursing career paths.

Curaleaf Laboratories, the symposium's headline partner, used the day to launch a free prescriber education platform. Jan Armstrong, its head of sales and commercial, said the modules are accredited for continuing professional development and cover foundations, clinical practice, and specialist pain, neurology and psychiatry, with an advisory board drawn from the UK, Germany, Poland, Sweden and Spain. Curaleaf put the number of people in the UK who self-medicate with cannabis for a medical condition at an estimated 1.8 million.
## Driving and work remain the patient's risk

Patient Protect founder Alex Fraser said most of the group's casework concerns driving: regular patients often test above the THC limit, so a positive roadside swab usually leads to arrest and a blood test at the station. He said 25% to 30% of its cases are dropped by prosecutors before court. Employment cases are the hardest to win, he said. The group plans a £5-a-month subscription and its first patient-discrimination report in January.

Richard List of the Association of Police Controlled Drug Liaison Officers, author of the national police guidance approved in October 2025, said officers often do not know medical cannabis is legal and that roadside test kits cannot tell prescribed from illicit cannabis. Driving guidance is being reviewed with a King's Counsel and has no date, and the first national online police training runs next year, as we reported on 22 November.

Watch for the overdue ACMD review and whether it addresses prescribing concentration. Watch Patient Protect's first discrimination report in January 2027, and the police driving guidance. For operators, the signal is whether clinics adopt the CIC's nursing model, which would widen the prescriber base without new legislation.
